{"id": "30:39/q26", "question": "When was this verse revealed relative to ribā's prohibition?", "turns_on": "Whether chronology favors an early warning or a Medinan legal setting.", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q26/p1", "position": "It is an early mention that condemns ribā before the later explicit legal ban.", "reasons": "Asad calls it the first mention; he and Study Quran date 2:275–281 to the final revelation, with ʿUmar saying its implications were not explained. Kuran Yolu calls this a first signal; Elmalılı says it censured Thaqīf's interest before prohibition."}, {"id": "30:39/q26/p2", "position": "The verse and preceding verse appear Medinan.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī sets aside reports or claimed consensus for Meccan dating; on a Medinan setting he reads forbidden usury and obligatory alms, while a Meccan setting favors lawful gifts and voluntary charity."}]}
{"id": "30:39/q27", "question": "What legal and moral scope does condemnation of ribā have?", "turns_on": "How far a moral condemnation can settle legal cases before or apart from explicit later prohibition.", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q27/p1", "position": "Interest-bearing loans and forbidden exchanges fall under ribā.", "reasons": "Early jurists broadly prohibited interest loans regardless of rate or motive, according to Asad. Bursawī includes same-kind excess and deferred exchange and says renaming a loan gift does not legalize it; necessity may excuse a compelled borrower. Ālūsī says many infer prohibition here."}, {"id": "30:39/q27/p2", "position": "The definition turns on exploitative, risk-free gain and changing economic conditions.", "reasons": "Asad notes no comprehensive agreed definition, cites Ibn Kathīr's difficulty and ʿUmar's uncertainty, and emphasizes weaker borrowers, lender-guaranteed gain and equitable risk sharing; he says generations must reinterpret cases. Islahi contrasts risk-bearing trade with gain from needy borrowers."}, {"id": "30:39/q27/p3", "position": "The verse implies prohibition even if the immediate phrase describes a gift.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says figurative gifts are censured by analogy and even more strongly imply prohibition of usury; Ālūsī objects that the same inference would also reach the usually permitted gift. Kuran Yolu notes the verse has no explicit ban."}]}
{"id": "30:39/q28", "question": "How is ribā pronounced at pause?", "turns_on": "Transmitted recitation versus grammatical accounts of pause alif.", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q28/p1", "position": "The transmitted pause is with yāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī cites al-Dānī's sole explicit Warsh report, claimed consensus and his teachers' practice; he prefers it as sound analogy."}, {"id": "30:39/q28/p2", "position": "Some grammarians permit opening tanwīn or a between-vowels pause.", "reasons": "Al-Shāṭibī and al-Sakhāwī transmit unrestricted fatḥ or intermediate sound, but Ibn al-Jazarī rejects it as analogy unattested in qirāʾāt manuals. Al-Māzinī says pause alif replaces tanwīn; al-Kisāʾī, Kufans and some Basrans say it restores the original final letter."}]}
{"id": "30:39/q29", "question": "Why is zakāt written with wāw?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q29/p1", "position": "It marks the universal category promised multiplication.", "reasons": "Burhān contrasts its universal scope in God's judgment with the local ribā written with alif."}]}
{"id": "30:39/q30", "question": "What does the final report about the Prophet's family say?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q30/p1", "position": "His family are called the word of piety and path of guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās transmits a sermon describing them also as the highest example, greatest proof and firmest bond."}]}
{"id": "30:39/q31", "question": "Who gives to whom in the first address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q31/p1", "position": "Some among those addressed give to others.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the act of giving necessarily has both donor and recipient within the plural address."}]}
{"id": "30:39/q32", "question": "What is the alif written after the wāw of ليربوا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q32/p1", "position": "It is an authoritative written form, not a plural marker.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says readers agree it does not mark a plural, despite the letter's appearance after wāw."}]}
{"id": "30:39/q33", "question": "What causes the charitable giver's reward to multiply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:39/q33/p1", "position": "God multiplies a gift directed to Him; resisting self-interest deepens its merit.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr contrasts return-seeking giving with zakat seeking God's face, for which God multiplies recompense. Qushayrī adds that mastering the self against its preferences earns divine recompense."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q01", "question": "Who are those asked whether they see?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q01/p1", "position": "The polytheists, especially the disbelievers among Quraysh.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām identifies the addressees as polytheists; Study Quran specifies disbelievers among Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q02", "question": "Does 'see' here mean physical sight or knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether the observable water and crops make the verb a reference to eyesight or to intellectual recognition.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q02/p1", "position": "It means literal, perceptible sight.", "reasons": "Bursevī prefers this because the process is perceptible and the ending again asks about seeing; al-Ālūsī describes the question as asking whether they have witnessed the sign."}, {"id": "32:27/q02/p2", "position": "It means knowing.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports this explanation from al-Baḥr al-ʿulūm, while choosing literal sight."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q03", "question": "What does 'drive' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q03/p1", "position": "To urge or move something onward.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī give the lexical gloss; al-Ṭabrisī adds sāqahu yasūquhu. Ṭabāṭabāʾī relays the gloss from Majmaʿ al-Bayān."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q04", "question": "How is water driven to the barren land?", "turns_on": "Whether the water is viewed as rain carried in clouds, flood runoff, or water conveyed in channels and springs.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q04/p1", "position": "By driving rain-bearing clouds, with rain or snow falling on the land.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says the rain travels in driven clouds. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says even river water originates in clouds. Bursevī distinguishes God's driving clouds from people's directing rivers. Al-Ālūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī also describe driven clouds; al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī include rain and snow."}, {"id": "32:27/q04/p2", "position": "By floods or torrents that bring water from elsewhere.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies a torrent and ineffective local rain; al-Ṭabrisī mentions dry high settlements; Ibn al-Jawzī includes rain and flood. Al-Wāḥidī allows rain or torrent on the general reading. Al-Ālūsī reports floods as a separate explanation."}, {"id": "32:27/q04/p3", "position": "Through rivers and springs, including running water from mountains.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī give this alongside rain and snow. Al-Nasafī includes rivers with rain; Ibn Kathīr mentions rivers and descending mountain water; al-Biqāʿī allows water from the earth; al-Ālūsī reports rivers and springs."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q05", "question": "What does al-jurz mean of the land?", "turns_on": "Whether barrenness means a present lack of plants after drought or grazing, or an inherent inability to grow despite the verse's crops.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q05/p1", "position": "Dry, barren land with no vegetation.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it smooth; Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba stress hard, dry ground, and the latter gives plural ajrāz and sunūn ajrāz for drought years. Al-Ṭabarī calls it hard and dry; Qatāda says dusty; ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say thirsty or dead; Ibn ʿAbbās says rain is ineffective except floodwater. Several cite 18:8. Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects that simply saying it produces nothing is imprecise."}, {"id": "32:27/q05/p2", "position": "Land whose former vegetation was cut, consumed, or dried away, but can grow again.", "reasons": "Ibn Shajara says its crops and trees were consumed; Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains thirst consuming growth and cites poetry. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, Bursevī and al-Kashshāf mention drought or grazing, rejecting salt flats because crops emerge. Al-Bayḍāwī explicitly prefers this over land that never grows. Al-Biqāʿī adds drying and crushing leave a smooth surface. Al-Rāghib describes vegetation cut at the root or eaten bare."}, {"id": "32:27/q05/p3", "position": "Naturally infertile salt-flat land.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this sense to al-Rāghib but rejects it here because the verse says crops grow; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī likewise exclude salt flats."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q06", "question": "What does the root of al-jurz evoke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q06/p1", "position": "Cutting or consuming everything until nothing remains.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī, al-Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī compare a voracious camel or person and a cutting sword. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabrisī cite rajaz lines; al-Māwardī's eater consumes dates with pits. Al-Thaʿlabī adds locusts that consume crops. Al-Zajjāj distinguishes jazūz for a voracious woman and jarāz for a sword. Al-Rāghib adds a proverb of total consumption and severe coughing."}]}

Ibn Kathīr says Egypt is included, describing its soft, heavy, saline, sandy soil, the Nile's rain-fed overflow and red silt that permits yearly crops; he does not limit the verse to Egypt."}, {"id": "32:27/q07/p5", "position": "A land in Babel.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī attributes this identification to Mujāhid."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q08", "question": "Does the definite article in al-jurz allow a specific place-name?", "turns_on": "Whether al-jurz is functioning as an adjective, an inherited descriptive name, or an ordinary proper name.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q08/p1", "position": "It may mark a descriptive adjective or a place-name transferred from a common description.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says jurz is an adjective that can take the article. Al-Mubarrad allows transferred descriptive names such as al-Madīna and al-Baṣra, whose article retains the earlier descriptive sense. Al-Qurṭubī favors the Yemen identification because Ibn ʿAbbās's report is sound and jurz can be a definite adjective."}, {"id": "32:27/q08/p2", "position": "The article suggests a particular land but is unexpected in a strict proper name.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Yazīd observes that the article suggests a specific land while a general reading remains possible; al-Mubarrad questions a proper name with the article, though he allows descriptive names to retain it. Al-Qurṭubī reports his doubt."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q09", "question": "What is the form of jurz and how is it vocalized?", "turns_on": "Vowel or silence on the rāʾ, and whether the recorded forms count as readings or dialectal variants.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q09/p1", "position": "The usual reading has a vowel on the rāʾ, commonly ḍamma; several dialectal vocalizations are allowed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the ḍamma reading the majority's. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī enumerate four forms, with al-Ṭabarī assigning fatḥ to Banū Tamīm. Al-Zajjāj reports several undiacritized forms and treats two as dialects; al-Naḥḥās lists jarz, jaraz and jurz. Comparisons include bukhl, raghb and rahb. Al-Jishumī counts three forms; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī count four."}, {"id": "32:27/q09/p2", "position": "A variant leaves the rāʾ silent as a lightened form.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj calls it a lighter form; Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes a report to him. Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī record the variant; al-Samīn points to discussion at the beginning of al-Kahf."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q10", "question": "How does al-jurz work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q10/p1", "position": "It may be a verbal noun used as an adjective for land with plant-consuming force.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj proposes this analysis and describes the land as having plant-consuming activity."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q11", "question": "How is 'so We bring forth' connected to what precedes?", "turns_on": "The syntactic connection of the raised verb and the causal implication that an imagined subjunctive would create.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q11/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with 'We drive'.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī list coordination as one possible syntax. Al-Zamakhsharī says the raised verb establishes actual greening; Ibn al-Khabbāz says the water, rather than seeing the water, causes it."}, {"id": "32:27/q11/p2", "position": "It begins a new clause disconnected from the preceding syntax.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī both list this analysis."}, {"id": "32:27/q11/p3", "position": "A hypothetical subjunctive would tie bringing forth to the seeing, spoiling the intended meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says it would reverse the point and imply failure to give thanks. Ibn al-Khabbāz says seeing water does not cause greening; water does."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q12", "question": "What does 'by it' refer to, and how does water bring crops forth?", "turns_on": "Whether 'by water' describes direct productive agency or the occasion on which God creates growth.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q12/p1", "position": "It refers to the water, with the verse presenting water as the means of growth.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī identify the antecedent. Al-Biqāʿī says water mixes with earth and draws real plants from its depths, unlike a magician's illusion. Al-Ālūsī reports that early authorities take the apparent sense."}, {"id": "32:27/q12/p2", "position": "God creates the crop when water arrives, without water directly producing it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this causal reading to the Ashʿarites."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q13", "question": "What does zarʿ include here?", "turns_on": "Whether the named principal crop stands for all plant growth or retains its familiar narrower sense.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q13/p1", "position": "Vegetation generally, including crops and other useful plants.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say crops are singled out as honored and principal but stand for all vegetation, since livestock eat other growth. Al-Ālūsī includes trees, and reports al-Baḥr allowing the broader sense; al-Biqāʿī also treats the passage as vegetation generally."}, {"id": "32:27/q13/p2", "position": "Cultivated crops in the familiar sense, named for their importance and honor.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports al-Baḥr's alternative: cultivated crops are the main purpose of growth and thus singled out."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q14", "question": "What is the grammatical form of zarʿ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q14/p1", "position": "It is originally a verbal noun used for the thing planted.", "reasons": "Bursevī and al-Ālūsī state this; Ṭabāṭabāʾī repeats the explanation from Majmaʿ al-Bayān."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q15", "question": "What do livestock and people eat from the growth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q15/p1", "position": "Livestock eat fodder, leaves, straw or grass, and sometimes grain; people eat grains, other staples, greens, roots and fruit.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and al-Nasafī contrast animal grass or stalks with human grain. Al-Qurṭubī adds herbage, greens and fruit; al-Bayḍāwī mentions figs and foliage. Al-Biqāʿī includes animal grain and people's green roots; Bursevī and al-Ālūsī add straw, legumes and fruit. Muqātil, al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn al-Jawzī state the shared benefit broadly."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q16", "question": "Why are livestock named before people?", "turns_on": "Whether sequence follows timing, dependence, rank, or the immediate crop context and its contrast with ʿAbasa.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q16/p1", "position": "Livestock eat the growth sooner, before it fruits or the grain is harvested.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says animals graze as soon as plants appear; al-Ālūsī says they eat before fruit and grain."}, {"id": "32:27/q16/p2", "position": "Livestock depend more exclusively on this growth and sustain human livelihood.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports animals eat fodder while people have other food. Al-Ālūsī says their food is limited to the growth; al-Biqāʿī says livestock sustain people's livelihoods and bodies."}, {"id": "32:27/q16/p3", "position": "The order rises from lower creatures to the more noble humans.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this; al-Ālūsī also gives the progression to the children of Adam."}, {"id": "32:27/q16/p4", "position": "The preceding mention of crops suits mentioning livestock feed first.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī gives this contextual reason in three notes. Al-Biqāʿī contrasts ʿAbasa, which follows food through to the human meal and names foods unsuitable for livestock; al-Sāmarrāʾī likewise says ʿAbasa discusses human food before fodder."}]}

{"id": "32:27/q22", "question": "Why does this verse end by asking whether they see?", "turns_on": "Whether the change from hearing to seeing follows the kind of evidence or intensifies the warning.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q22/p1", "position": "The revival and provision are visible, while the previous verse's destroyed nations are known by hearing.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Burhān, al-Ālūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī compare 32:26. {"id": "32:27/q23", "question": "What does the visible revival teach?", "turns_on": "The notes draw several compatible lessons from the same visible sign: resurrection, divine power and provision, and reproach for ignoring it.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q23/p1", "position": "God can resurrect dead people as He revives dead land.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī, Asad and Study Quran give this analogy. {"id": "32:27/q26", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding passage and sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes identify different levels of context: adjacent signs, the sūra's paired denials, and the closing warning.", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q26/p1", "position": "It shifts from destroyed past peoples to a visible creation sign supporting resurrection.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān contrasts the earlier destroyed nations with the new evidence of God's power. {"id": "32:27/q27", "question": "What Nile incident is reported alongside the Egypt interpretation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q27/p1", "position": "After Egypt's conquest, ʿAmr stopped drowning a dressed virgin annually; ʿUmar's letter invoking God was followed by a sixteen-cubit overnight Nile rise.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits the account through Ibn Lahīʿa and Qays ibn Ḥajjāj; it says the custom ended afterward."}]}
{"id": "32:27/q28", "question": "What is reported about the sūra's place of revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q28/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Sajdah is Makkan.", "reasons": "Study Quran states this in its introduction."}]}

{"id": "32:27/q30", "question": "How is the preceding verse parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:27/q30/p1", "position": "In 32:26, yahdi has an implicit subject supplied by “how many We destroyed”; kam is the object of ahlaknā, and yamshūn is circumstantial.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives this parsing of the verse immediately before 32:27."}]}

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported with this pair by Abū Ḥayyān and Alūsī; the latter calls prayer a synecdoche for tasbīḥ and prefers the dawn and afternoon pair over it."}, {"id": "33:42/q01/p9", "position": "Perform all prayers or acts of worship.", "reasons": "Kashshāf says every obedience and good deed may count as remembrance, with all prayers as especially excellent glorification. Abū Ḥayyān likewise encompasses every obedience and singles out prayer. Alūsī reports an extension to all obedience and prayer at all times but calls it remote."}, {"id": "33:42/q01/p10", "position": "Pray or invoke God in the morning and evening without naming a specific rite.", "reasons": "Ibn Ḥayyān's gloss is praying to God at these times; al-Durr reports Muqātil as dawn and dusk prayer. Study Quran reports prayer and invocation from dawn to sunrise and from sunset to night prayer."}, {"id": "33:42/q01/p11", "position": "Perform supererogatory prayer or devotions, including night vigil.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says optional prayer is possible, which changes the relation between this command and general remembrance. Qurṭubī gives a variant poetic example recalling Yūsuf calling on his Lord."}, {"id": "33:42/q01/p13", "position": "Perform afternoon and the two evening prayers.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī reports this attribution to Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "33:42/q01/p14", "position": "Glorify through the acts, attributes, and Essence in an inward sense.", "reasons": "Qāshānī's inward reading calls for transcendence of acts, attributes, and Essence."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q02", "question": "What do bukra and aṣīl mean as times of day?", "turns_on": "The issue is whether the terms are ordinary day periods, prayer designations, or a particular lexical form of aṣīl.", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q02/p1", "position": "Aṣīl is the late afternoon or evening from ʿaṣr until night.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, al-Akhfash and Abū Ḥayyān define this span; Majāz gives late afternoon until night for the phrase. Qurṭubī repeats al-Mubarrad's account."}, {"id": "33:42/q02/p2", "position": "The beginning and end of the day.", "reasons": "Nasafī, Biqāʿī, Bursevī, Alūsī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī define the pair this way; Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes the later part as after ʿAṣr. Ibn ʿĀshūr says al-bukra is daybreak and al-aṣīl the late afternoon after ʿaṣr."}, {"id": "33:42/q02/p3", "position": "Aṣl is a plural of aṣīl.", "reasons": "Another grammarian compares the singular ragīf and plural rughuf; this differs from al-Mubarrad's account of aṣl as a synonym."}, {"id": "33:42/q02/p4", "position": "On the prayer reading, bukra is Fajr.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says the prayer interpreters agree that morning is Fajr; Baghawī also identifies it."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q03", "question": "Do the two time words limit the command or imply a wider span?", "turns_on": "The sources either take the endpoints as a figure for continuous practice or emphasize the stated periods themselves; several combine both.", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q03/p1", "position": "They name the two ends to imply remembrance and glorification through the whole day or at all times.", "reasons": "Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān treat the ends as all time. Biqāʿī includes both busy and resting periods, Bursevī stresses the endpoints and their special honor, and Elmalılı compares a Turkish expression. Ibn ʿAbbās says remembrance has no set limit or ordinary excuse save loss of reason; al-Ṭabarī adds remembrance in every condition and consequent blessings from God and angels. Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares 41:38; Study Quran points to 6:52, 18:28, 19:11, 24:36 and 48:9."}, {"id": "33:42/q03/p2", "position": "They direct believers to actual morning and evening remembrance.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī describes early morning and evening practice; Ibn Kathīr compares 30:17–18, which names evening, morning and other parts of the day. {"id": "33:42/q04", "question": "Why are morning and evening especially mentioned?", "turns_on": "The reasons offered are angelic witnessing, the times' practical difficulty or honor, their symbolism, and the rhetorical value of spanning different hours.", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q04/p1", "position": "They are virtuous times witnessed by the changing angels of night and day.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī calls the times excellent and witnessed; Nasafī and Alūsī say the angels meet then. Ṭabrisī ties the angelic meeting specifically to dawn and night prayers."}, {"id": "33:42/q04/p2", "position": "The prayers at these times require special effort amid rest or work.", "reasons": "Kashshāf says dawn and the evening pair are difficult to perform and observe; Abū Ḥayyān speaks of dawn and night. Biqāʿī says dawn and afternoon kept despite competing rest and work show love of worship."}, {"id": "33:42/q04/p3", "position": "They encompass different states of activity and encourage remembrance in both.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī notes that the day's beginning and end encompass busy and resting periods. Ibn ʿĀshūr says naming both fills the day's portions as far as possible."}, {"id": "33:42/q04/p4", "position": "They are familiar, honored hours for devotion.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says these are well-known times; Bursevī says God distributes provision, sends blessings and answers prayers between dawn and sunrise, so people should attend to that hour."}, {"id": "33:42/q04/p5", "position": "The two terms vary the wording so that remembrance stays fresh.", "reasons": "Qushayrī explains the double expression this way."}, {"id": "33:42/q04/p6", "position": "Dusk recalls the world's end and dawn the resurrection.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says both times are witnessed by angels and also signify the Hour."}, {"id": "33:42/q04/p7", "position": "The periods suit glorifying God beyond changing conditions and defects.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects the changing day to divine transcendence of change and passing defects."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q05", "question": "How do the time adverbs relate grammatically to the two commands?", "turns_on": "The disagreement is whether the time phrase governs both coordinated imperatives or only the second, whose predecessor already demands frequent remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q05/p1", "position": "They modify both the command to remember and the command to glorify.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī and Alūsī compare 'fast and pray on Friday'; Ibn ʿĀshūr says both words are adverbial with both commands."}, {"id": "33:42/q05/p2", "position": "They are accusative adverbs of time.", "reasons": "Jishumī identifies the case and adverbial function."}, {"id": "33:42/q05/p3", "position": "They attach to glorification while abundant remembrance already covers most times.", "reasons": "Alūsī reasons that if much remembrance in 33:41 means remembrance through most times, the first command does not need the two adverbs."}]}
